Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Alex had been on the sales floor of the regional retail chain for five years, his life organized around the rhythm of opening hours and the predictable shuffle of customers. One blistering June afternoon, while he was restocking a display of canned soups, the refrigeration unit behind the register sputtered and erupted in a sudden, thunderous explosion. The blast sent glass and metal shards scattering across the aisle, and the sound of shattering plastic rang through the entire building. He felt the floor tremble under his feet and was forced to stumble back as a stack of boxes toppled onto the floor. The metallic tang of broken metal lodged in his memory, the texture of each shard pressed against his skin, and the chaos of people screaming and pushing—an abrupt moral violation of the calm, orderly environment he had known—left him shaken and terrified. The next day, Alex walked into the store with his heart pounding, the very sight of the familiar aisle layout a trigger that pulled him back into that terrifying instant. When the fluorescent lights buzzed and he heard a customer loudly complaining about a malfunctioning display, he felt a sudden wave of dread wash over him. To quell the anxiety that swelled in his chest, he would whisper to himself that the incident “probably never really happened” or “wasn’t that bad,” a form of magical thinking that allowed him to distance himself from the event. Simultaneously, he would force himself to “just ignore it,” pushing any recollections or thoughts of the blast deep into the recesses of his mind in a desperate attempt to suppress them. When Alex reached for a cardboard box to replace a missing shelf item, the rough, uneven surface of the cardboard felt oddly familiar. The tactile sensation, the same grainy texture he had felt against his fingers during the explosion, jolted a vivid image into his consciousness: the sudden flash of light, the sharp crack of metal, the panic of customers. This physical proximity to a texture that mirrored the one from the day he was crushed under falling goods was a trigger that reawakened the memory with startling clarity. The memory arrived in Alex’s mind as a series of still images, each a snapshot of the day’s horror, the most intense detail being the scream of a customer, the sharp clang of metal, the flash of broken glass. The shame that flooded his chest as he recalled his own trembling and the way he had fled the aisle was so overpowering that he resorted to cutting his wrist in the privacy of the break room. The sharp pain was a brief, albeit crude, distraction that allowed him to step back from the relentless onslaught of that memory. Even as he did this, he would repeat the mantra that the event had “never been that bad,” a magical belief that simultaneously prevented him from fully processing the traumatic image and kept it alive in the same distorted form. The shame associated with recalling the explosion drove Alex to avoid any setting that might remind him of that day. He no longer entered the back stockroom, a place where the same type of cardboard and metal shelving hung in a configuration that mirrored the disaster scene. Even the mere thought of customers misbehaving—shouting, pushing—would set his heart racing as he imagined another chaotic moment. His avoidance of these spaces was fueled by the memory itself; the recollection of that day, wrapped in shame, kept feeding his fear that proximity would repeat itself. The self-harm and suppression tactics Alex employed did not dissolve the memory; rather, they anchored it more firmly. Each time he cut, the brief relief it offered was immediately followed by a surge of memory, the snapshot of the blast replaying with a vividness that seemed more real than his everyday experiences. The act of denying the event’s significance through magical thinking ensured that the memory stayed raw, refusing to integrate into a broader, more manageable narrative. As a result, Alex’s internal dialogue became a loop: each self-harm episode led to a reinforced, unprocessed memory, which in turn fed back into his strategies to avoid and suppress, perpetuating the cycle. In the weeks that followed, Alex’s attempts to suppress his thoughts would backfire. The anxiety that rose from trying to silence the memory would crack open with new spikes of fear, causing him to notice every customer’s irritated frown or any slight misstep on the floor as if it were a potential trigger. This heightened threat monitoring only intensified his avoidance and magical thinking, setting the stage for a relentless cycle of fear, avoidance, and self-harm. It was this cumulative distress—his nightly insomnia, the weight of isolation from his wife, the constant dread of returning to the aisles—that finally pushed Alex to seek help. He was terrified that the cycle would never end, yet he hoped that through therapy he could learn to let the memory settle and reclaim his workplace without it consuming him.
